It'd be good to solve this in tandem with https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2368. It looks like there @rniwa was in agreement with you that the Firefox behavior is better.

It seems like the proposal is to truncate the event path for all mouse events (and pointer events?) to remove disabled form controls, and any of their (shadow-including??) parents.

@annevk, can you think of any way to spec this without modifying event dispatch?

The current spec seems to be advocating for a third behavior, which is to *don't dispatch the event* when the target would be a disabled form control. This would result in clicking on children of a disabled button firing the event, but in that case the event should reach the disabled form control (since dispatch was not prevented). And no browsers seem to follow that.

The current spec is nice and simple and does not need to get into the innards of event dispatch; it just serves as input into the question of whether or not to dispatch. But, it's probably not good for web developers, and it's not what anyone implements, so oh well.

It seems reasonable to not-dispatch a click event if it's performed on a disabled button. "click" is pretty much an activation event, but a disabled button cannot be activated.

Dispatching "click" but skipping the button in the event path is weird.

Looks like in Chrome disabled button is in the composedPath, but event listeners aren't called on it. So one can't rely on event.composedPath() to return the targets on which listeners will be called.

> Have other browsers gotten bug reports about the behavior they have?

I've seen several bugs about child elements of `<fieldset disabled>`, which I suppose is similar enough to child elements of `<button disabled>`:
- https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1245511
- https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=588760

> What is stable Chrome behavior? Propagating click from child elements of a disable button to the ancestor of the button, but not firing on the button itself. That is just weird. I'm rather strongly against such behavior. I don't think we have other cases where we drop magically an item from the event path. (But I could add that implementing Chrome's behavior in Gecko should be very easy, one would just change the parent target, if the default parent was disabled)

Based on this and the supportive comments, I suppose that the chrome/webkit behavior should not be what we end up with.

Should we do the firefox thing where we fire event listeners up to the disabled button, or should we not fire any listeners at all if there are any disabled field controls in the event path? I'll spell this out a little more clearly:

- Option 1: Fire listeners on parent and child elements of disabled form controls. This is what chrome and webkit currently do.
- Option 2: Fire listeners on child elements of disabled form controls, but not parents. This is what firefox currently does.
- Option 3: Don't fire any listeners on child or parents of disabled form controls.

Here is where the bugs stand on these options:
- [This crbug](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1245511) desires at least the child elements to get events, so option 1 or 2 would be work.
- [This crbug](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=588760) desires parent elements to not get events, so option 2 or 3 would be work.
- [This crbug](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1169799) desires child elements to get events, so option 1 or 2 would work.
- [This firefox bug](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1653882) that @saschanaz shared desired parent elements to get events, so only option 1 would work. Maybe they could look at pointer events instead...?

Based on these, **I think that option 2, the firefox behavior, is best**. Hopefully implementing this doesn't result in too many regression bugs.

> Looks like in Chrome disabled button is in the composedPath, but event listeners aren't called on it. So one can't rely on event.composedPath() to return the targets on which listeners will be called.

Yep, I see that firefox doesn't include the nodes which weren't fired on in composedPath. We will have to fix this in chrome and webkit as well. Perhaps composedPath should be tested in https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/32381

> https://github.com/webcompat/web-bugs/issues/65773

This bug made me realize that there is a significant difference in chrome with `<button disabled>` vs `<input disabled>`. Parent nodes of `<input disabled>` will always get `click` events, but parent nodes of `<button disabled>` will only get `click` events if a child node of the `<button>` is clicked. Perhaps this is because `<input>` has a shadow root with child nodes which actually receive the click events, but I'm not certain. Up until now I was only looking at `<button>`.

After skimming the rest of the bugs in this list, it looks like they are all about parent nodes of `<input disabled>`.

> I fear that it will. All the "See also" bugs in https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1653882 are the webcompat issues we got

I debugged the funny behavior with buttons vs buttons with children vs inputs and I found that it comes down to this:
https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/events/mouse_event.cc;l=373-386;drc=127616d9e079e19774925a56fdd29acd568d7329

Any time a disabled node is clicked, we don't dispatch the event at all. The reason this doesn't work for buttons with children or input elements is that the actual node you're clicking isn't a disabled form control. Input elements have a child node in their shadow dom which gets clicked.

The logic to skip disabled form controls in the event path is here: https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/dom/node.cc;l=2905-2918;drc=033ae102a356d906af6f62d3a31588f0b2fc4b18

Just for fun, I also traversed the blame to find where these two lines of code were introduced. They come from 2003 and 2005:
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/420c380f646feb11c39b3c3ef2730561b28fdeff%5E%21/
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/17f7fe709006d20caf0ecef81896fc56b6056427%5E%21/

The first change, which makes disabled form controls get skipped in the event path, was made to prevent disabled submit buttons from submitting forms. It's not clear why all mouse events were prevented, but it was at least acknowledged:
> Don't send mouse events for disabled elements. But we do want those events to pass through the bubble and capture phases, just avoid triggering any listeners on this node itself.

The second change, which prevents mouse events from getting dispatched at all when it starts exactly on a disabled form control element, appears to be part of a refactor. It's also not clear what the motivation is for preventing all mouse events.
> mouseover and mouseout have been patched not to fire when they occur on a disabled control.  More generally, no mouse event will be delivered to a disabled element.  The current check only examines the target node, and this is not good enough (but can be improved in a later patch).  Some nodes will be children of disabled ancestors (e.g., options or children of a button), and this is not yet taken into account.

I guess they already knew that button elements with children would act different, and they didn't end up improving in a later patch 😅

> I debugged the funny behavior with buttons vs buttons with children vs inputs and I found that it comes down to this:

@josepharhar this is the best, most comprehensive analysis I've seen about this issue. It should be linked by every relevant tickets on Chrome's codebase -- it's absolutely golden.

In the interest of making consistent behavior for disabled form controls which do or don't have child elements, I think these are our options:
- Option A: Always propagate click events even if the node which is being clicked is a disabled form control.
  - This is like "Option 1" from my previous comment but would also cause `<button disabled>hello world</button>` to propagate click events to parent nodes.
  - I imagine doing this in chrome would break fewer websites because it's more similar to what we are currently doing in chrome.
- Option B: Never propagate click events to parents above disabled form controls.
  - This is identical to "Option 2" from my previous comment.

I agree that Option B is the most ideal, but I'm still concerned about how much will break if we take away those events and I don't really know whats acceptable or not. I'll try adding a use counter for this scenario.

With these changes, will [using `pointer-events: none;`](https://stackoverflow.com/a/66029445/6867099) continue to allow click events to bubble up to the parent?

(Use case: data table with disabled `<input>` fields in some cells; clicking anywhere in a row is expected to fire the `<tr>`'s onclick handler. Ref: https://github.com/desec-io/desec-stack/pull/660)

Based on my experimenting here with the new browser behavior: https://jsfiddle.net/jarhar/u9pdk5xf/
It looks like adding pointer-events:none actually causes click events to be fired. This seems odd to me, but is this the desired behavior for you?
That seems reasonable behavior to me. pointer-events:none basically removes the element from hit-testing, so its parent becomes the target.

> It looks like adding pointer-events:none actually causes click events to be fired. This seems odd to me, but is this the desired behavior for you?

Yes, it is the intended behavior for us. -- In fact, the mechanism doesn't matter (I don't feel that it has to be done via `pointer-events: none`). What's important to us that there is *some* way to have the parent of a disabled form field receive the click event.

It's true that a disabled form field has no business dealing with click events. However, it's quite evident that when such a field is contained in a table row, or some other kind of box, then the user would think to have clicked the row or the surrounding box whenever they click what's in it (including a disabled form field). The parent therefore needs a way to handle the click. (If no action is desired, figuring that out is the parent event handler's business.)

A negative side-effect of `pointer-events: none` is that it renders text selection (clicking and dragging the mouse pointer) inside the disabled form field impossible. It would be nice if there be a way to pass the click event to the disabled field's parent, without disabling text selection. (Those things, I feel, should have nothing to do with each other; using `pointer-events` to remove the element from hit-testing is only a workaround.)

This is just extra food for thinking. I don't feel strongly about the text selection issue. That doesn't mean it's not a problem for others.

I recommend listening for `pointerup` and/or `pointerdown` events instead of `click` events for disabled form controls. I can't think of any other workarounds like `pointer-events:none` and I don't think we will ever start firing `click` events on disabled form controls.

> I recommend listening for `pointerup` and/or `pointerdown` events instead of `click` events

`pointerup` and `pointerdown` fire when at least one mouse button starts getting pressed or once no button is pressed anymore, respectively. In particular, it does not distinguish between left/right button etc. Semantically, that's no replacement for a `click` event.

> I don't think we will ever start firing `click` events on disabled form controls

That's fine. I believe the issue is about firing the `click` event on the parent element (e.g. table row), which is not disabled.

> That's fine. I believe the issue is about firing the `click` event on the parent element (e.g. table row), which is not disabled.

Not firing `click` means the parent element won't get it either, so it matters.

I sometimes wonder a new event `pointerclick` that fires strictly on clicks by pointer devices would help here, but I guess `click` is an activation event for a some good reason.

Perhaps I'm lacking some knowledge here. I understand why clicks are not handled directly by disabled form fields (well, they are disabled, so they don't interact). But what is the reasoning for not allowing that event to reach the parent element (as Chrome has been handling it, and still does in its stable release)?

Reading the thread above, the argument I saw is in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5886#issuecomment-1169022612, which says:
> [This crbug](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=588760) desires parent elements to not get events

However, there are several other reports that desire the opposite, such as https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1107929 or https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1653882 (there are some more in Mozilla's bug tracker). Other parts of the community have the same irritation, e.g. https://stackoverflow.com/q/48904638/6867099 and other StackOverflow posts.

So, obviously, there are competing desires. Now the interesting part is that when the browser *does* let the parent handle the event, it is possible for the parent's event handler to look at the situation and decide to do nothing. Conversely, when the browser inhibits event processing, all bets are off and there is no remedy (besides the CSS kludge, which has other unintended side effects such as affecting text selection behavior).

Given the contradicting desires that cannot be both fulfilled, the one situation which has no remedy (= not bubbling clicks to the parent) seems worse than the one where, although the event does arrive at the parent, you can still implement a no-op handler for this case. Anyone who wants the opposite behavior could be told to catch the event at the parent, investigate where it originated, and (in case it was the disabled child) just return.

So, with all this is in mind, I wondering what piece of info I'm lack in order to understand why one would not allow click event bubbling on disabled form elements.

> Use case: data table with disabled `<input>` fields in some cells

> So, with all this is in mind, I wondering what piece of info I'm lack in order to understand why one would not allow click event bubbling on disabled form elements.

I think that not firing the click event is pretty central to the idea of the disabled attribute preventing activation behavior, at least for button-like form control elements. The fact that chromium and webkit send click events to ancestor elements of disabled input elements was almost certainly a mistake that we are trying to fix so that the disabled attribute functions consistently across form control elements. @smaug---- seemed to [dislike this behavior](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5886#issuecomment-1168605988).

I haven't quite gotten the new behavior to stable chrome yet so there is still a chance that it will break websites so badly that I won't be able to ship the new behavior.

What if you used `readonly` instead of `disabled` on your input elements? I'm also guessing that firefox has never exhibited the behavior you want for `<input disabled>`, right?

> > Use case: data table with disabled `<input>` fields in some cells
> 
> > So, with all this is in mind, I wondering what piece of info I'm lack in order to understand why one would not allow click event bubbling on disabled form elements.
> 
> I think that not firing the click event is pretty central to the idea of the disabled attribute preventing activation behavior, at least for button-like form control elements.

What's the reason for this opinon?

> @smaug---- seemed to [dislike this behavior](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5886#issuecomment-1168605988).

@smaug---- disliked it stating "Propagating click from child elements of a disable button to the ancestor of the button, but not firing on the button itself. That is just weird. I'm rather strongly against such behavior. I don't think we have other cases where we drop magically an item from the event path."

I agree that this would be unreasonable behavior.  However, the case that @smaug---- dislikes (propagating click events from children of the button to the ancestor without firing on the button itself) is **different** from what I'm talking about.

It seems to me that when a button is disabled, then we should not only drop the single button element from the event path, but rather: the button, including its children (!), don't listen to click events, because the "button box" is *disabled* as a whole.

That does not, however, preclude the event from being dispatched to the first parent. I want to retain the parent half and only drop the child side of the event path.

It *is* legit to fire a click handler of a `<div>` or a `<tr>` if you click *anywhere* inside that element. Why would that be different? Why would not any pixel in that box reach that parent's click handler, even when there happens to be a disabled form field or button at that pixel?

That disabled field should play no role with regards to the parent nothing the click within its box.

> What if you used `readonly` instead of `disabled` on your input elements?

`readonly` does not fully disable the input element. For example, for a text field, the mouse pointer over this field will change to a caret cursor, whereas for a disabled field, the disabled field does not impact the cursor display. There are other rendering differences as well.

Of course, all of that can be worked around with a bunch of CSS. That's ugly, but not really the point. My point is that there is, in itself, a legitimate use case to *disable* the form field, without effectively disabling any the parent's event handlers.

When a field is disabled, it should behave as if it were not there, in as many regards as possible. It is still displayed, of course, but otherwise it should be irrelevant to the rest of the page. It is just plain unclear to me why one would want a disabled text field to affect the parent's `onclick` handler.

> I'm also guessing that firefox has never exhibited the behavior you want for `<input disabled>`, right?

That's correct. There are a bunch of people (including me) considering this a bug, see my Bugzilla references in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5886#issuecomment-1413872593. Firefox' unexpected behavior is the reason why I found this issue.

---

In the end, I think we don't need to argue what Chrome does or what Firefox does or what workarounds exist. We need to argue:

1. Is there is a reason to prevent a click on a `<tr>` element to fire *that* elements `onclick` handler, just because the pointer position *within* the `<tr>` happens to be on disabled form field? -- Obviously, we don't want to fire the form field's handler when it is disabled. However, I guess there is no doubt that the table row has been clicked. Can anyone come up with a good reason not to fire the table row's click handler in this case?
2. If such reasons can be found, why would they not apply to `pointerup` and `pointerdown`, as noted [here](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5886#issuecomment-1407045835)?

>I want to retain the parent half and only drop the child side of the event path.

No browser drops the child side of the event path. Retaining the parent side means the exact behavior smaug disliked in that case.

IMO the point here is that it's weird to skip some arbitrary part of the path while still keeping the propagation.

`z-index` is for layer, but `disabled` is not really for manipulating the event path. HTML seemingly has no textual description what `disabled` semantically means, but [MDN does](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/:disabled):

>The :disabled [CSS](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS) [pseudo-class](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Pseudo-classes) represents any disabled element. An element is disabled if it can't be activated (selected, clicked on, typed into, etc.) or accept focus. The element also has an enabled state, in which it can be activated or accept focus.

And since the event propagation starts from the child to the parent, it's natural that any trial to interact with a disabled element won't propagate any event to the parent (because it's not in a state that can emit any event). If you want some limited interaction, `readonly` sounds like a better choice as @josepharhar said in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5886#issuecomment-1421660579.

Edit: Or `pointer-events: none` as you mentioned above.

>A negative side-effect of pointer-events: none is that it renders text selection (clicking and dragging the mouse pointer) inside the disabled form field impossible.

But `disabled` does that too, right?

This was recently un-flagged in Chrome and unfortunately our application (an electronic health record) [was one of the casualties](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1422096). The effect for our users is that they can no longer prescribe medications for their patients. They still can't, because I get to spend my night writing and deploying a fix (if it's possible to make the change that quickly, given how our application is architected). Reading the thread I get the sense that there were no perfect ways forward to unify the behavior across browsers. What would have helped us is if this was visible in `chrome://flags` so we could at least give our users a workaround while we work on a fix. I do appreciate the tough decisions you all make and how it is impossible to cater to [every possible use case](https://xkcd.com/1172/). </vent>

After reading through https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1422096 and https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1422547 I'm wondering if we should tweak the behavior I implemented for bubbling on disabled fieldsets. I believe that this is also the issue which the previous comment discovered. Consider the following: ```html
click me!
``` The way that we implemented this in chrome and firefox will prevent click events from propagating above the disabled fieldset, which has broken some sites and I'm not sure is really great behavior. [This bug](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1422547#c1) also pointed out that frameworks like React only add an event listener for bubbling events to the root element, which increases the likelihood that this is breaking. Disabled fieldsets should make their descendant form control elements become disabled and not fire click events, but should we really stop event propagation at the fieldset element itself even when a non-form control element is clicked? I propose that we continue event propagation when encountering disabled fieldsets. @smaug---- what do you think? I have disabled the new behavior in chrome for now.

An issue has cropped up where someone wants click events to fire on their disabled textarea, and pointer-events:none isn't good enough for them because that makes selection stop working in the textarea: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1474913

I recommended that they listen to pointerup and fire click events in response to pointerup on the parent of the disabled textarea

we were relying on click events bubbling from a disabled input in our web application and came across https://www.reddit.com/r/HTML/comments/163vrs2/event_bubbling_on_disabled_input_broken_in_last/ and https://support.google.com/chrome/thread/231546184/click-event-not-working-on-disabled-input?hl=en when we got bug reports about that no longer working. i also came across [this suggestion](https://stackoverflow.com/a/32058918/333625) to apply `pointer-events: none` to disabled inputs (e.g. `input[disabled] { pointer-events: none }` to prevent mouse events from being swallowed by the disabled input. is there a better mitigation strategy you all would recommend to allow mouse events to still be captured from ancestor elements of a disabled input, or does that seem like the best approach?

the sentiment expressed in the reddit thread is an expectation that this is a regression that they hope will be patched in the future. their workaround is creating an empty div covering the input that captures and propagates mouse events.

EDIT GitHub had collapsed comments about this from earlier. i just found https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5886#issuecomment-1407045835 where @josepharhar recommends listening to `pointerup` / `pointerdown` events instead of mouse events (as well as other discussions about using `pointer-events: none` and its effect on text selection). sorry for the noise!
